metadata.title: Exploring Influencing Factors at Student and Teacher/School Levels on Science Self-efficacy Using Machine Learning and Multilevel Latent Profile Analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 science data and constructs the dependent variable (science self-efficacy) from PISA WLE scores transformed to an international metric. The analytic sample is restricted to five high-performing countries (Singapore, Japan, Estonia, Finland, South Korea) and further excludes students who did not respond to science self-efficacy items (926 excluded). For predictors, variables with ≥50% missingness are deleted, and remaining missing values are imputed using MICE repeated 10 times. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) in the ML models; given the use of PyCaret regression models and the explicit deletion of “weights” from the variable pool, weighting is likely not incorporated into the predictive modeling stage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science-focused data for 15-year-olds from five selected high-performing countries (Singapore, Japan, Estonia, Finland, South Korea) out of 72 participating countries. Excluded 926 students who did not respond to science self-efficacy items, retaining 28,886 students from 971 schools. From an initial pool of 195 candidate predictors (110 student-level, 75 teacher/school-level), deleted variables irrelevant for analysis (e.g., personal identification, weights, and hard-to-include code/subjective response variables) and removed predictors with ≥50% missingness. For remaining predictors, applied MICE multiple imputation (Light Gradient Boosting Machine model) repeated 10 times; normalized variables to a common scale and removed one variable from any pair with correlation ≥0.900 to reduce multicollinearity.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds; five countries: SGP, JPN, EST, FIN, KOR)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Student level (n=17,562 train / 4,622 test): Light Gradient Boosting — RMSE=0.960, R2=0.356, MAE=0.675; Gradient Boosting regressor — RMSE=0.964, R2=0.351; Extra Trees regressor — RMSE=0.969, R2=0.344; Bayesian Ridge — RMSE=0.974, R2=0.338; Ridge regression — RMSE=0.985, R2=0.322. Teacher/school level (n=17,521 train / 4,622 test): Gradient Boosting regressor — RMSE=1.172, R2=0.041; AdaBoost regressor — RMSE=1.178, R2=0.031; Bayesian Ridge — RMSE=1.178, R2=0.030.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data from Singapore, Japan, Estonia, Finland, and South Korea, the study leveraged environmental awareness, science activities, epistemological beliefs, interest in broad science topics, and test anxiety to predict students’ science self-efficacy (WLE score), finding that LightGBM achieved the lowest student-level RMSE (0.960) among compared regression models. This indicates that affective and motivational science-related factors (especially environmental awareness and reduced test anxiety) are consistently predictive of science self-efficacy in high-performing science contexts, though the study’s predictive importance does not establish causal direction and survey-weight use is not reported.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed PISA 2015 science data for 15-year-olds from five high-performing countries (SGP, JPN, EST, FIN, KOR), excluding 926 students with missing science self-efficacy responses and retaining 28,886 students from 971 schools. Science self-efficacy was measured using PISA science self-efficacy items (8 Likert items) scaled as WLE scores and standardized to an international metric (mean 0, SD 1). For prediction, the authors compared 20+ regression models in PyCaret with an 8:2 train/test split and 10-fold CV grid search; at the student level, LightGBM was best with RMSE=0.960 and R²=0.356, while teacher/school-level prediction was weaker (best Gradient Boosting RMSE=1.172, R²=0.041). Top student-level predictors included environmental awareness, science activities, epistemological beliefs, interest in broad science topics, and test anxiety, and MLPA further classified students into low/moderate/high self-efficacy profiles. Limitations include the absence of reported complex-survey weighting in ML models and the fact that feature importance and profile associations are predictive rather than causal.
